stories.headline: Building resilience not a one-time exercise, must keep at it: FM
stories.title: Building resilience not a one-time exercise, must keep at it: FM
stories.summary: Uncertainty is now a standing condition of the global economy and policy must be designed around it, said Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman.“We need to keep building resilience as we go along; it is not a one-time exercise,” she said at the fifth Kautilya Economic Conclave in New Delhi on Saturday.The conclave, organised by the Institute of Economic Growth in partnership with the finance ministry, is being held from October 3-5 under the theme “Resilience in an Age of Flux”.The FM exhorted economists to look beyond headline growth when they judge how an economy handles shocks.The evidence of resilience is often counterfactual, it lies in the outcomes that did not materialise, she said. “…An inflation spiral that did not take hold, queues that did not form at fuel outlets, banking stress that did not surface and a fiscal correction that was never forced.”“These counterfactuals deserve as much attention from economists as the headline growth rate,” she said.The world has seen primarily two kinds of shocks over the past four years: crude price spikes and tighter US monetary conditions, she said.Also Read: India’s inflation inches closer to 5 percent. Is an October rate hike imminent?“The conflicts involving Russia, Ukraine and Iran, and the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, added a new kind of shock, one that threatened the physical movement of oil and gas as well as their prices.”These shocks arrived at a time when the world had thin buffers.Global public debt rose to nearly 94 percent of GDP in 2025 and is projected to reach 100 percent by 2029, a level previously seen only after the Second World War.India has managed the weather these shocks well, she said.India’s economy grew 7.8 percent in the April-June (Q1) quarter of this fiscal when current account deficit (CAD) was 0.5 percent of GDP. Bad loans at banks are at a multi-decade low, and foreign-exchange reserves are about $766 billion.The FM listed the government’s focus on efficient last-mile delivery, infra spending, reforms, fiscal prudence, entrepreneurship, and the capacity to maintain economic continuity through disruption as some of the steps that have helped build resilience.On the future challenges, she said India approaches the coming years from a position of strength.Building resilient supply chains and global openness are two of the key priorities. “Global economic relationships must remain open, predictable, and rules-based,” the FM said.On the impact of AI on jobs, Sitharaman called for skilling the young people and urged industry to take a greater role in designing and delivering training.Also, private sector must now take over from the government as the main driver of investment, including spending on research and development (R&D), she said.The government has carried the capital spending cycle for most of the past decade.India spends 0.83 percent of GDP on R&D, compared with 2.7 percent across the OECD. Private companies account for only about 36 percent of that spending, she said.Her remarks add to the government’s long-standing push for companies to invest more.The government has budgeted Rs 12.2 lakh crore for capex in the Union Budget for FY27.Sitharaman highlighted the Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) scheme the government has designed to support the shift as India moves from “Made in India” to “Imagined and Made in India”.

opening: Uncertainty is now a standing condition of the global economy and policy must be designed around it, said Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman.
“We need to keep building resilience as we go along; it is not a one-time exercise,” she said at the fifth Kautilya Economic Conclave in New Delhi on Saturday.
body: The conclave, organised by the Institute of Economic Growth in partnership with the finance ministry, is being held from October 3-5 under the theme “Resilience in an Age of Flux”.
The FM exhorted economists to look beyond headline growth when they judge how an economy handles shocks.
The evidence of resilience is often counterfactual, it lies in the outcomes that did not materialise, she said.

“…An inflation spiral that did not take hold, queues that did not form at fuel outlets, banking stress that did not surface and a fiscal correction that was never forced.”“These counterfactuals deserve as much attention from economists as the headline growth rate,” she said.
The world has seen primarily two kinds of shocks over the past four years: crude price spikes and tighter US monetary conditions, she said..
Is an October rate hike imminent?

“The conflicts involving Russia, Ukraine and Iran, and the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, added a new kind of shock, one that threatened the physical movement of oil and gas as well as their prices.” These shocks arrived at a time when the world had thin buffers.
Global public debt rose to nearly 94 percent of GDP in 2025 and is projected to reach 100 percent by 2029, a level previously seen only after the Second World War.
India has managed the weather these shocks well, she said.
India’s economy grew 7.8 percent in the April-June (Q1) quarter of this fiscal when current account deficit (CAD) was 0.5 percent of GDP.
Bad loans at banks are at a multi-decade low, and foreign-exchange reserves are about $766 billion.

The FM listed the government’s focus on efficient last-mile delivery, infra spending, reforms, fiscal prudence, entrepreneurship, and the capacity to maintain economic continuity through disruption as some of the steps that have helped build resilience.
On the future challenges, she said India approaches the coming years from a position of strength.
Building resilient supply chains and global openness are two of the key priorities.
“Global economic relationships must remain open, predictable, and rules-based,” the FM said.
On the impact of AI on jobs, Sitharaman called for skilling the young people and urged industry to take a greater role in designing and delivering training.
Also, private sector must now take over from the government as the main driver of investment, including spending on research and development (R&D), she said.
The government has carried the capital spending cycle for most of the past decade.
India spends 0.83 percent of GDP on R&D, compared with 2.7 percent across the OECD.
Her remarks add to the government’s long-standing push for companies to invest more.
The government has budgeted Rs 12.2 lakh crore for capex in the Union Budget for FY27.

Sitharaman highlighted the Rs 1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) scheme the government has designed to support the shift as India moves from “Made in India” to “Imagined and Made in India”.

stories.headline: Tighter financial conditions could spill over to banks, warns Sanjay Malhotra
stories.title: Tighter financial conditions could spill over to banks, warns Sanjay Malhotra
stories.summary: Any tightening of global financial conditions could spill over to banks and other markets, Reserve Bank of India Governor Sanjay Malhotra said at the fifth Kautilya economic conclave in New Delhi, flagging rising leverage and stretched valuations as the main channels of risk.“High leverage in pursuit of high returns, and this is particularly true of the advanced economies [where] hedge funds, option sellers, exchange trade, traded funds, and other non-bank financial intermediaries have expanded leverage both in equity and bond markets,” he said, adding that rising leverage is a sign of maturing financial cycle. However, this is of “concern” especially since equity valuations are stretched and bank and NBFI interconnectedness has deepened both on the liability as well as on the asset side.Speaking on the interplay of monetary policy and financial stability, Malhotra further said that the RBI does not use monetary policy to address financial stability risks. “We follow the separation principle, monetary policy for price stability and targeted regulatory, supervisory, and macroprudential tools, where financial stability risks are identified.”He also noted that the financial system had absorbed the supply shock due to the West Asia conflict “quite well” and growth has been resilient.“However, the global economic environment continues to remain challenging. The conflict has exacerbated not only inflationary pressures but it has also elevated financial system vulnerabilities,” he added.Also Read: West Asia tensions begin filtering into Indian economy, says Finance MinistryThe RBI governor identified five global vulnerabilities. Global debt has risen, maturities have shortened and bond yields have hardened sharply, which could squeeze sovereign finances, strain corporate debt servicing and hit bank balance sheets through bond losses. Emerging markets with heavy non-resident holdings of sovereign debt could face outflows if carry trades unwind.Second, AI-linked asset valuations could be sharply repriced if the investment cycle slows. “As the investment cycle matures, any slowdown in AI investment or earnings could trigger a sharp repricing of financial assets, especially in the AI value chain. High risk appetite has spurred an increase in leverage, which, along with [a potential] decline in cash flow among major AI firms would further amplify market corrections and financial market volatility,” he added.Third, hedge funds, option sellers, ETFs and other non-bank intermediaries have built up leverage, deepening links with banks. Fourth, private credit has shown weak lending standards in some high-profile defaults. Fifth, AI is heightening cyber risk in a borderless financial system. Each may be manageable alone, he said, but a simultaneous hit could strain the global financial architecture.“Large differences in cyber capabilities and resilience and resolution capabilities across countries have implications for jurisdictions far beyond the source of the vulnerability,” he noted.For India, Malhotra said the exposure runs mainly through higher commodity prices and external-sector pressures. But he said the economy is navigating the phase from strength, with inflation averaging 2 percent last year and the fastest growth among major economies. Government bond yields have risen only partially, which he credited to fiscal consolidation and credible monetary policy. Equities have corrected from high valuations, but in an orderly fashion. An AI-led correction abroad could even draw capital inflows to India, he added.Malhotra called for better data, scenario analysis and system-wide resilience. “Today’s resilience may not necessarily imply tomorrow’s immunity,” he said.

opening: Any tightening of global financial conditions could spill over to banks and other markets, Reserve Bank of India Governor Sanjay Malhotra said at the fifth Kautilya economic conclave in New Delhi, flagging rising leverage and stretched valuations as the main channels of risk.

“High leverage in pursuit of high returns, and this is particularly true of the advanced economies [where] hedge funds, option sellers, exchange trade, traded funds, and other non-bank financial intermediaries have expanded leverage both in equity and bond markets,” he said, adding that rising leverage is a sign of maturing financial cycle.
body: However, this is of “concern” especially since equity valuations are stretched and bank and NBFI interconnectedness has deepened both on the liability as well as on the asset side.
Speaking on the interplay of monetary policy and financial stability, Malhotra further said that the RBI does not use monetary policy to address financial stability risks.

“We follow the separation principle, monetary policy for price stability and targeted regulatory, supervisory, and macroprudential tools, where financial stability risks are identified.” He also noted that the financial system had absorbed the supply shock due to the West Asia conflict “quite well” and growth has been resilient.
The conflict has exacerbated not only inflationary pressures but it has also elevated financial system vulnerabilities,” he added.
The RBI governor identified five global vulnerabilities.

Global debt has risen, maturities have shortened and bond yields have hardened sharply, which could squeeze sovereign finances, strain corporate debt servicing and hit bank balance sheets through bond losses.
Emerging markets with heavy non-resident holdings of sovereign debt could face outflows if carry trades unwind.
Second, AI-linked asset valuations could be sharply repriced if the investment cycle slows.
“As the investment cycle matures, any slowdown in AI investment or earnings could trigger a sharp repricing of financial assets, especially in the AI value chain.

High risk appetite has spurred an increase in leverage, which, along with [a potential] decline in cash flow among major AI firms would further amplify market corrections and financial market volatility,” he added.
Third, hedge funds, option sellers, ETFs and other non-bank intermediaries have built up leverage, deepening links with banks.
Fourth, private credit has shown weak lending standards in some high-profile defaults.
Fifth, AI is heightening cyber risk in a borderless financial system.
Each may be manageable alone, he said, but a simultaneous hit could strain the global financial architecture.
“Large differences in cyber capabilities and resilience and resolution capabilities across countries have implications for jurisdictions far beyond the source of the vulnerability,” he noted.
For India, Malhotra said the exposure runs mainly through higher commodity prices and external-sector pressures.
But he said the economy is navigating the phase from strength, with inflation averaging 2 percent last year and the fastest growth among major economies.
Government bond yields have risen only partially, which he credited to fiscal consolidation and credible monetary policy.
Equities have corrected from high valuations, but in an orderly fashion.
An AI-led correction abroad could even draw capital inflows to India, he added.
Malhotra called for better data, scenario analysis and system-wide resilience.
“Today’s resilience may not necessarily imply tomorrow’s immunity,” he said.

stories.title: Uttarakhand Cabinet approves bill to replace 153-year-old British-era irrigation law

article_sentences: The Uttarakhand Cabinet decided to repeal the colonial-era canal law and bring a new irrigation Bill.
The move came alongside reforms in private university norms and medical college pay as the government held its first cabinet meeting in Champawat.

The Uttarakhand Cabinet on Sunday decided to repeal the 153-year-old British-era Northern India Canal and Drainage Act, 1873, and replace it with a new state law suited to Uttarakhand's geographical conditions, officials said.

The cabinet also approved changes to the policy and standards for setting up private universities and cleared a revision in salaries and honorariums for senior residents, junior residents and demonstrators in government medical colleges.
The decisions were taken at a cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami at the NHPC complex in Banbasa in Champawat district.
Officials said the cabinet decided to table the Uttarakhand Irrigation and Drainage Bill, 2026, in the Assembly.
This was the first time a state cabinet meeting was held in Champawat, the chief minister's Assembly constituency.
According to a statement, the cabinet approved amendments to the policy and standards governing the establishment of private universities.
Under the revised framework, a minimum built-up area of 2,500 square metres in hilly regions and 20,000 square metres in plain areas will be required.
It was also decided to work out separate evaluation criteria to ensure quality in proposals for setting up private universities.
In view of the shortage of senior residents, junior residents and demonstrators in government medical colleges, the cabinet approved a revision of their payable salaries and honorariums.

Dhami said cabinet meetings would no longer be confined to Dehradun and would be held in different places to directly place local issues, development prospects and regional priorities before the government.
